Democratic Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs has selected former Republican Mayor John Giles, now independent, as her running mate. In Minnesota, progressive Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan won the Democratic Senate primary by 20 points over moderate Rep. Angie Craig, in a race defined by anti-ICE anger following the Trump administration's immigration crackdown. Flanagan, backed by Bernie Sanders and Ilhan Omar, could become the first Native woman in the Senate. Her win is the latest in a series of progressive victories over moderates in the Midwest — including Abdul El-Sayed's Michigan U.S. Senate primary win the prior week — and marks a second straight primary setback for Democratic Senate Leader Chuck Schumer. Former TV sports reporter Michele Tafoya won the Republican Senate primary in Minnesota and will face Flanagan in November. Ilhan Omar has been projected to win the Democratic primary in Minnesota's 5th Congressional District. Sen. Amy Klobuchar has been projected to win the Minnesota DFL gubernatorial primary and will face Minnesota House Speaker Lisa Demuth in November; Demuth defeated Trump-backed MyPillow founder Mike Lindell, who received roughly 31% of the vote. In Minnesota's 1st Congressional District, GOP incumbent Brad Finstad survived a primary against challengers Gregory Goetzman and Oliver Morlan. In Connecticut, former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin has been projected to defeat veteran Democratic incumbent Rep. John Larson in the House primary. In Wisconsin, Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley defeated democratic socialist Francesca Hong in a stunningly narrow Democratic gubernatorial primary — winning by less than a percentage point — after re-entering the race and securing an endorsement from outgoing Gov. Tony Evers. Crowley, who could become the state's first Black governor, will face Republican Rep. Tom Tiffany in November. Following her loss, Hong endorsed Crowley, saying her campaign was not about getting one person into office. Sabato's Crystal Ball subsequently shifted the Wisconsin governor's race toward Democrats. In South Carolina's special GOP Senate primary, Darline Graham (32.6%) and Rep. Ralph Norman (24%) have advanced to an Aug. 25 runoff, with Rep. Russell Fry finishing third at 20.3%. Trump-backed Graham denied being a "nepo senator." An analysis by G. Elliott Morris found that primary election polls miss by an average of 13 points, and prediction markets were also shown to have failed on the Hong result in Wisconsin.
